question_en: She ______ in Delhi since 2015.
explanation_en: “Since 2015” marks a period continuing up to now, so the present perfect continuous (has been living) is used. Simple past “lived” would mean she no longer lives there.

question_en: By the time the police arrived, the thieves ______.
explanation_en: Of two past actions, the earlier one takes the past perfect (had + V3). Escaping happened before the police arrived.

question_en: I ______ the report by tomorrow evening.
explanation_en: “By + future time” shows completion before a future moment, which needs the future perfect (will have + V3).

question_en: Look! The children ______ in the garden.
explanation_en: “Look!” signals an action happening at this moment, so the present continuous is required.

question_en: If I ______ you, I would accept the offer.
explanation_en: In an unreal (second) conditional, the if-clause takes the subjunctive “were” for all persons: If I were you, ... would.

question_en: The train ______ before we reached the station.
explanation_en: The train’s departure happened earlier than our arrival (both in the past), so the past perfect is used for the earlier action.

question_en: The teacher told the class that the earth ______ round the sun.
explanation_en: A universal or scientific truth stays in the simple present even after a past-tense reporting verb.

question_en: Hardly ______ the room when the phone rang.
explanation_en: “Hardly/Scarcely/No sooner” is followed by the past perfect, with auxiliary–subject inversion: Hardly had she entered ... when ...

question_en: I ______ this film three times.
explanation_en: Repeated experience up to the present with no fixed past time takes the present perfect (have seen).

question_en: How long ______ you ______ for the bus?
explanation_en: “How long” with an action that began in the past and continues now takes the present perfect continuous: have you been waiting.

question_en: This time next week, we ______ on the beach in Goa.
explanation_en: “This time next week” refers to an action in progress at a specific future moment, so the future continuous (will be lying) is used.

question_en: He is ______ honest man.
explanation_en: “Honest” begins with a silent h, so it has a vowel sound and takes “an”.

question_en: ______ Ganga is the holiest river of India.
explanation_en: Names of rivers take the definite article “the”.

question_en: She plays ______ guitar very well.
explanation_en: “The” is used before the names of musical instruments when we speak of playing them: play the guitar.

question_en: My brother is studying at ______ university in Pune.
explanation_en: “University” begins with the consonant sound /yu/, so the article is “a”, not “an”.

question_en: She has ______ MBA degree from a reputed institute.
explanation_en: “MBA” is pronounced “em-bee-ay”, beginning with a vowel sound, so “an” is used.

question_en: Rohan goes to ______ school by bus every day.
explanation_en: When a place is visited for its primary purpose (school for studying), no article is used: goes to school.

question_en: What ______ pity that he failed again!
explanation_en: In exclamations with a singular countable noun, “What a/an + noun” is used: What a pity!

question_en: She is ______ European who has settled in Chennai.
explanation_en: “European” starts with the consonant sound /yoo/, so “a” is correct despite the initial vowel letter.

question_en: She is very good ______ mathematics.
explanation_en: The fixed phrase is “good at” a subject or skill.

question_en: The teacher congratulated him ______ his success.
explanation_en: The verb “congratulate” takes “on” with the achievement: congratulated him on his success.

question_en: She is married ______ a doctor.
explanation_en: “Married to” a person is the correct collocation.

question_en: She is suffering ______ high fever.
explanation_en: We suffer from a disease or illness, so “suffering from” is used.

question_en: The Principal was annoyed ______ the students for coming late.
explanation_en: “Annoyed with” is used for a person (annoyed at/about a thing).

question_en: Divide the sweets ______ the three children equally.
explanation_en: “Among” is used for more than two persons or things; “between” is for two.

question_en: Aman is senior ______ me by two years.
explanation_en: Words such as senior, junior, superior, inferior, prefer take “to”, not “than”.

question_en: The old man was accused ______ theft.
explanation_en: “Accuse” is followed by “of”: accused of theft.

question_en: I prefer tea ______ coffee.
explanation_en: “Prefer” is always followed by “to”, never “than”.

question_en: Beware ______ pickpockets in crowded places.
explanation_en: The verb “beware” takes “of”: Beware of pickpockets.

question_en: Neither the manager nor the employees ______ present in the meeting.
explanation_en: In “neither...nor”, the verb agrees with the noun nearest to it. “Employees” is plural, so “were”.

question_en: Each of the boys ______ given a prize.
explanation_en: “Each” is singular and takes a singular verb, even when followed by “of + plural noun”.

question_en: Mathematics ______ my favourite subject.
explanation_en: Subjects ending in -ics (mathematics, physics, economics) are treated as singular.

question_en: The number of applicants ______ increasing every year.
explanation_en: “The number of” is singular (the number is increasing); “a number of” would be plural.

question_en: Either of the two answers ______ correct.
explanation_en: “Either” means one of the two and is singular, so it takes “is”.

question_en: Bread and butter ______ my usual breakfast.
explanation_en: Two nouns that form one idea (bread and butter, rice and curry) take a singular verb.

question_en: Ten kilometres ______ a long distance to walk.
explanation_en: A plural expression of distance, money, time or weight used as a single unit takes a singular verb.

question_en: The Principal as well as the teachers ______ invited to the function.
explanation_en: With “as well as”, “along with”, “together with”, the verb agrees with the first subject (Principal – singular).

question_en: Many a student ______ failed in this test.
explanation_en: “Many a” is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb: Many a student has failed.

question_en: The police ______ investigating the case.
explanation_en: “Police” is a collective noun that is always plural in usage, so it takes a plural verb.

question_en: Change the voice: ‘The police arrested the thief.’

options.en: The thief was arrested by the police.
The thief is arrested by the police.
The thief had been arrested by the police.
The police was arrested by the thief.

explanation_en: Simple past active becomes was/were + V3 in the passive; the object becomes the subject.

question_en: Change the voice: ‘The students completed the project.’

options.en: The project is completed by the students.
The project has been completed by the students.
The project was completed by the students.
The students were completed by the project.

explanation_en: Simple past: object + was/were + V3 + by + agent.

question_en: Change the voice: ‘Who wrote this letter?’

options.en: By whom is this letter written?
By whom has this letter been written?
By whom was this letter written?

explanation_en: For a 'Who' question in the active voice, the passive begins 'By whom', and the tense is kept: simple past 'wrote' becomes 'was written'. 'Has been written' changes the tense.

question_en: Change the voice: ‘She is writing a novel.’

options.en: A novel is being written by her.
A novel is written by her.
A novel was being written by her.
A novel has been written by her.

explanation_en: Present continuous passive = is/am/are + being + V3.

question_en: Change the voice: ‘They will have finished the work by noon.’

options.en: The work will be finished by them by noon.
The work will have been finished by them by noon.
The work would have been finished by them by noon.
The work has been finished by them by noon.

explanation_en: Future perfect passive = will have been + V3.

question_en: Change the voice: ‘Someone has stolen my bicycle.’

options.en: My bicycle was stolen by someone.

explanation_en: Present perfect passive = has/have been + V3; the vague agent ‘someone’ is normally omitted.

question_en: Change the voice: ‘Do it at once.’

options.en: Let it be done at once.

explanation_en: Imperative sentences become passive with ‘Let + object + be + V3’.

question_en: Change into the active voice: ‘The window was broken by the boy.’

options.en: The boy has broken the window.
The boy was breaking the window.

explanation_en: Simple past passive (was broken) becomes simple past active (broke).

question_en: Change into the active voice: ‘A letter was being written by Neha.’
explanation_en: Past continuous passive (was being written) corresponds to past continuous active (was writing).

question_en: Change into indirect speech: He said, “I am happy.”

options.en: He said that he was happy.
He said that he is happy.
He said that I was happy.
He said that he had been happy.

explanation_en: Present simple becomes past simple in reported speech when the reporting verb is in the past; pronoun I changes to he.

question_en: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, “Where do you live?”

options.en: She asked me where I lived.
She told me where did I live.
She asked me where do you live.
She asked me that where I lived.

explanation_en: A wh-question is reported with ‘asked’, statement word order and no ‘that’.

question_en: Change into indirect speech: The teacher said, “The earth moves round the sun.”

options.en: The teacher said that the earth moved round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth had moved round the sun.
The teacher told that the earth moves round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth moves round the sun.

explanation_en: A universal truth does not change tense in indirect speech.

question_en: Change into indirect speech: He said to her, “Please help me.”

options.en: He ordered her to help him.
He requested her to help him.
He said her to help me.
He asked that she helps him.

explanation_en: A polite request with ‘please’ is reported with ‘requested’ + to-infinitive.

question_en: Change into indirect speech: “Alas! I have failed,” said the boy.

options.en: The boy said that alas he has failed.
The boy exclaimed that I had failed.
The boy exclaimed sorrowfully that he had failed.
The boy asked sorrowfully whether he had failed.

explanation_en: Exclamations are reported with ‘exclaimed with joy/sorrow’; present perfect shifts to past perfect.

question_en: Change into direct speech: He asked me if I had finished my work.

options.en: He said to me, “Have you finished my work?”
He said to me, “Had I finished my work?”
He said to me, “Have you finished your work?”
He said to me, “Have I finished your work?”

explanation_en: The 'if' clause shows a yes/no question; the past perfect in the report goes back to the present perfect, and the pronouns change I → you and my → your: “Have you finished your work?”.

question_en: Change into indirect speech: She said, “I will come tomorrow.”

options.en: She said that she would come the next day.
She said that she will come tomorrow.
She said that I would come tomorrow.
She said that she would come tomorrow.

explanation_en: Will becomes would and tomorrow becomes the next day / the following day.

question_en: Change into indirect speech: The captain said to the team, “Let us play carefully.”

options.en: The captain said to the team that let us play carefully.
The captain proposed to the team that they should play carefully.
The captain ordered the team to play carefully.
The captain asked the team that we play carefully.

explanation_en: ‘Let us’ expresses a suggestion and is reported with ‘proposed/suggested that ... should’.

question_en:
Choose the most appropriate question tag for the blank.
Let's go for a walk after dinner, ______?
explanation_en: A sentence beginning with 'Let's' (a suggestion that includes the speaker) always takes the tag 'shall we?'. 'Will we' and 'don't we' do not fit a suggestion.

question_en:
Choose the most appropriate question tag for the blank.
Nobody called me while I was out, ______?
explanation_en: 'Nobody' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive; indefinite pronouns like nobody, everyone and someone are picked up by 'they'. Hence 'did they?'.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
______ he worked very hard, he could not clear the examination.
explanation_en: The two clauses contrast (hard work, yet failure), so a concessive conjunction is needed: 'Although'. 'Because' shows cause, 'unless' a condition and 'whether' a choice.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The roses in your garden smell ______.
explanation_en: 'Smell' here is a linking verb (like look, feel, taste, seem), so it is followed by an adjective describing the subject: 'smell sweet'. An adverb is used only with an action verb, e.g. 'He chewed slowly'.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Despite of the heavy rain / the match / was played / as scheduled.
explanation_en: “Despite” is never followed by “of”. Correct: Despite the heavy rain (or In spite of the heavy rain).

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
She told me / that she / didn’t knew / the answer.
explanation_en: After “did/didn’t”, the main verb takes its base form: didn’t know.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
The furniture in the new office / are made / of teak wood / and looks elegant.

options.en: The furniture in the new office

explanation_en: “Furniture” is an uncountable, singular noun, so the verb should be “is made”.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error. If there is no error, select option 4.
He is taller / than any other boy / in his class.
explanation_en: The comparative with “any other + singular noun” is correct, so the sentence has no error.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
I have been knowing / him since / we were children / in the same school.
explanation_en: “Know” is a stative verb and is not used in continuous tenses. Correct: I have known him since ...

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Hardly had he reached / the station / than the train / left without him.
explanation_en: “Hardly” is followed by “when”, not “than” (“No sooner” takes “than”).

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Rahul is one of the boys / who has / won medals / in the national games.

options.en: Rahul is one of the boys

explanation_en: In “one of the + plural noun + who”, the relative pronoun refers to the plural noun, so the verb is “have”.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
She gave me / a very good advices / on how to / prepare for the interview.
explanation_en: “Advice” is uncountable and has no plural form. Correct: a piece of advice / very good advice.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
The Principal, along with / the teachers, / are planning / a farewell party.
explanation_en: The subject “Principal” is singular; “along with” does not make it plural. Use “is planning”.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Between you and I, / the project / is not likely / to succeed.
explanation_en: A preposition takes the objective case: “Between you and me”.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error. If there is no error, select option 4.
The book that / I bought yesterday / is very interesting.
explanation_en: The sentence is grammatically correct; the relative clause and verb agree properly.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
My uncle / is working / in this company / since 2010.
explanation_en: “Since 2010” needs the present perfect continuous: has been working.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
Though he was tired, / but he / continued working / on the project.
explanation_en: “Though” and “but” should not be used together in one sentence. Remove “but”.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error.
I prefer / walking than / driving to / the office.
explanation_en: “Prefer” takes “to”: I prefer walking to driving.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
She [hardly never] visits her native village.
explanation_en: “Hardly” already has a negative sense, so “never” cannot be added. The correct idiom is “hardly ever”.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
I [am living] in Jaipur since my childhood.
explanation_en: “Since + point of time” with an action continuing now needs the present perfect continuous: have been living.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
The teacher asked the boy [why was he late].
explanation_en: In reported questions the word order becomes that of a statement (subject before verb): why he was late.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
He suggested [me to take] a taxi.
explanation_en: “Suggest” is not followed by an object + to-infinitive. It takes a that-clause (that I take / that I should take) or a gerund.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
Each of the girls [have] brought her own lunch.
explanation_en: “Each” is singular and needs “has”.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
The cost of living [have risen] sharply this year.
explanation_en: The subject “cost” is singular, so the verb must be “has risen”.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
I would have helped you [if you would have asked].
explanation_en: In the third conditional, the if-clause uses the past perfect (if + had + V3) and the main clause uses would have + V3.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
She is [more taller] than her sister.
explanation_en: A one-syllable adjective forms the comparative with -er; “more” must not be added (double comparative).

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
He [is knowing] the answer to every question.
explanation_en: “Know” is a stative verb and is not used in continuous forms; use the simple present.

question_en:
Select the option that best replaces the part in square brackets. If no change is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
Neither the teacher [or the students] were aware of the changes.
explanation_en: “Neither” is paired with “nor”, not “or”.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
Scarcely had I reached the gate [than the bell rang].
explanation_en: 'Scarcely' and 'Hardly' are paired with 'when' (or 'before'); only 'No sooner' takes 'than'. So the correct form is 'Scarcely had I reached the gate when the bell rang'.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
[Not only he is] a good singer but also a fine dancer.
explanation_en: When a sentence begins with 'Not only', the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion): 'Not only is he a good singer but also a fine dancer'. 'Does he' would need a main verb such as 'sing'.

question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
He has been / absent in the class / for the last / three days.
explanation_en: The adjective 'absent' takes 'from': 'absent from the class'. The other segments are correct.

question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
She looked / very much / beautiful / in the red saree.
explanation_en: 'Very' modifies an adjective in the positive degree (very beautiful); 'much' is used with comparatives and past participles (much better, much admired). So 'very much beautiful' is wrong.

question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The scenery / of Kashmir / are very / charming in spring.
explanation_en: 'Scenery' is an uncountable noun and is always singular, so the verb must be 'is very charming'. Similar nouns: furniture, luggage, information, advice.

question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
If he will come / tomorrow, / I shall discuss / the matter with him.
explanation_en: In a first conditional the if-clause takes the simple present even for a future idea: 'If he comes tomorrow, I shall discuss...'. 'Will' belongs only in the main clause.

question_en:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
He returned back / from Mumbai / late last night / by the express train.
explanation_en: 'Return' already means 'come back', so 'returned back' is redundant. Similar errors: repeat again, revert back, cousin brother.

question_en:
Identify the segment that contains an error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
The jury were divided / in their opinions / about the verdict.
explanation_en: A collective noun takes a plural verb when its members act as individuals with different views. 'The jury were divided in their opinions' is correct; 'their' confirms the plural sense.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
The doctor [wrote] a strong medicine for the patient's fever.
explanation_en: A doctor 'prescribes' medicine; 'prescribe' is the exact word for recommending a treatment. 'Described' means told about and 'subscribed' means paid for regularly.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
The Principal [laid stress over] the need for discipline in the morning assembly.
explanation_en: The fixed expression is 'lay stress on' (also 'lay emphasis on', 'insist on'). 'Over', 'at' and 'for' are not used with 'stress' in this sense.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
She [has been working] in this school for ten years and still loves her job.
explanation_en: 'For ten years' with an action that continues now ('still loves her job') needs the present perfect continuous, which is already used. So no substitution is required.

subtopic: Fill in the blanks – confusable words
question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The clever thief managed to ______ the police for a whole week.
explanation_en: 'Elude' means to escape or avoid being caught. 'Allude' means to refer indirectly, 'collude' to conspire secretly and 'exclude' to leave out.
